articles.title: Your WhatsApp AI Agent Works in a Demo. Here's What Breaks in Production.
articles.excerpt: An AI agent on WhatsApp demos beautifully. You paste in a business description, ask "what time do you open?", and it answers in one friendly sentence. Then real customers arrive. They ask about a comp…
articles.body: An AI agent on WhatsApp demos beautifully. You paste in a business description, ask "what time do you open?", and it answers in one friendly sentence. Then real customers arrive. They ask about a competitor's product, send voice notes, type "HUMAN!!" in capitals, fire three messages in five seconds, and reply to a three-day-old thread. The model provider has a bad afternoon. A customer asks the bot to ignore its instructions. This post goes through what we had to build around the model to run the AI agent in WAPGROWAI 's WhatsApp inbox, and the questions we think every team should settle before turning one on. The TypeScript snippets are small, simplified versions of the patterns, and each was run against the cases it describes. 1.

articles.excerpt: The number one rule of scaling is ensuring that you have more than enough resources readily available to consume, digest, and schedule what you need to run. In the case of agentic workloads, that's ty…
articles.body: The number one rule of scaling is ensuring that you have more than enough resources readily available to consume, digest, and schedule what you need to run. In the case of agentic workloads, that's typically Agents. For example, is there enough memory to run multi-Actor Workers? Or do you need to scale Workers out to schedule Actors accordingly? In this blog post, you'll learn how to schedule and scale Actors (where Agents run) via Workers and WorkerPools for any number of Actors that need to run within your environment. Prerequisites To follow along with this blog post from a hands-on perspective, you will need: A cluster with Agent Substrate running (e.g., GKE or a local cluster like Kind). Agentgateway set as the dataplane proxy for your atenet-router .

articles.title: The Hidden Cost of Unoptimized REST API Payloads in Node.js
articles.excerpt: Most REST API performance issues in Node.js apps don’t happen because of heavy queries. They happen because we send the entire database model down the wire when the client only needs two fields. Here…
articles.body: Most REST API performance issues in Node.js apps don’t happen because of heavy queries. They happen because we send the entire database model down the wire when the client only needs two fields. Here is what usually happens: • Database returns 50 columns with nested relations. • Mongoose or TypeORM serializes the whole object graph. • JSON.stringify blocks the Node.js event loop for 40ms. • Network bandwidth gets wasted on metadata the client discards. Fixing this isn't about rewriting in Rust or upgrading your AWS instance. It’s about intentional API design: Project your queries strictly at the SQL/ORM level using DTOs or explicit selects. Apply pagination limits by default — never trust SELECT * . Profile your JSON serialization overhead using clinic.js or built-in node --prof.

articles.body: Introduction Stack Overflow, once the undisputed hub for developers seeking answers to coding conundrums, is facing a reckoning. The platform’s toxic environment and rigid rules are driving users away, fueling a growing demand for alternatives. At the heart of this exodus lies a fundamental clash between the platform’s community moderation processes and the evolving expectations of its users. Developers, particularly newcomers, are increasingly frustrated by a system where strict rule enforcement often overshadows empathetic engagement . Consider the feedback loop triggered by Stack Overflow’s downvoting mechanism. A user posts a question that, while technically sound, fails to adhere to the platform’s billion bullshit rules —a phrase echoing the exasperation of many.

articles.title: Scientists discover 'chemical starter kit' for life in planetary birthplaces
articles.excerpt: The discovery of surprising molecules of methanol and associated maser activity has expanded the inventory of the chemical starter kit that builds planets in young star systems.
articles.body: Methanol, coming as part of the 'chemical starter kit' around young stars, has produced some unexpected surprises that could ultimately reveal some of the conditions in which planets and potentially life form around protostars. The methanol discoveries were made by astronomers using ALMA (the Atacama Large millimeter/submillimeter Array) in the Atacama Desert in Chile, as part of a project called COMPASS (the Complex Organic Molecules in Protostars with ALMA Spectral Surveys). "Our work provides insight into the complex chemistry of young star systems and is ultimately an important piece of the puzzle in understanding the origin of life," said University of Bern astrophysicist Maria Drozdovskaya, who leads the COMPASS project, in a statement .

articles.body: SpaceX wants to start flying its Starship megarocket a lot more often. The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is in the early stages of reviewing the request. Today (Oct. 14), the agency announced "its intent to prepare a Programmatic Environmental Impact Statement, open a public scoping period and hold public scoping meetings for SpaceX’s proposal." Starship, which stands more than 400 feet (122 meters) tall, is the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built. It's also designed to be fully and rapidly reusable, a breakthrough that SpaceX believes will revolutionize spaceflight.

articles.body: Mark Zuckerberg at the Meta Connect developer conference. | Photo: Andrej Sokolow/dpa/picture alliance via Getty Images Last week, Anthropic and OpenAI looked like they had the AI race to themselves, pulling ahead with increasingly powerful models that left their rivals in the dust. Google seemed hopelessly far behind, while Meta, despite spending billions to revive its floundering AI ambitions , had yet to establish itself as a serious contender. Even the latest models coming out of China , impressive as they were, appeared to be playing catch-up. Then, in the space of a few days, everything changed. Google and Meta both unveiled frontier models they claim can go toe to toe with the best from OpenAI and Anthropic.

articles.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
articles.excerpt: "Small weight-based replicators" could usher in a new generation of computer worms.
articles.body: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.
